**"The Ballad of Dusty Marvell, As Best I Can Remember It"**

Told by aging frontier midwife and chronic liar Henrietta "Hen" Pool—who frequently interrupts her own narrative to argue with the reader about what's actually true—this is the story of her best friend, Dusty Marvell, a half-Apache con woman who schemed her way from penniless drifter to the first female cattle baroness in New Mexico Territory, only to lose her empire, her name, and ultimately her life when the very lawlessness that built her fortune invited a brutal reckoning she refused to outrun. Hen narrates from a jail cell in 1893, addressing "whoever the hell finds this journal," oscillating between gut-punch grief and riotous, whiskey-soaked recollections of the twenty years she and Dusty spent as inseparable partners in audacious fraud—two women who built a language between them more fluent than any marriage, who could read each other's bluffs across a crowded saloon, and whose bond was the one honest thing in a life constructed entirely of lies. The core tension isn't whether Dusty's downfall is coming—Hen tells you on page one that it is—but whether Hen herself is telling this story to memorialize her friend or to confess her own role in destroying her, and whether the reader can trust a narrator who keeps crossing out sentences, rewriting her own history, and begging you not to judge either of them too harshly.

narrative_beats:
# Scene-Level Beat Sheet: "The Ballad of Dusty Marvell, As Best I Can Remember It"

---

## Beat 1: The Jail Cell Address — "Whoever the Hell Finds This Journal"

**Concrete Action:** Hen Pool establishes the frame. She is writing from a jail cell in 1893. She tells us her name, tells us she is a midwife and a liar (in that order or the reverse, depending on the day), and tells us that her best friend, Dusty Marvell, is dead. She announces this on the first page — not with elegy but with the blunt, pre-emptive exhaustion of someone who has been carrying the fact for long enough that it has become furniture. She tells the reader not to get comfortable. She tells the reader not to trust her. Then she begins telling the story anyway.

**Narrative Technique — The Pre-Ruined Narrative as Trust Paradox:** Hen's opening move is to dismantle every tool the reader normally relies on. She announces the ending (Dusty dies), discredits the narrator (she is a self-proclaimed liar), destabilizes the text itself (she is writing in a journal she expects to be found, not read — the audience is accidental), and explicitly tells you that what follows may not be true. This *should* make the reader disengage. Instead, it creates a paradox: a liar who tells you she's lying is, in that single act, telling the truth. Hen's opening gambit is the most honest thing she will say for a hundred pages, and the reader instinctively feels this. The confession disguised as a caveat is the structural seed of the entire story.

**What Makes It Memorable — The Reason for the Telling Is the Thing Being Hidden:** Hen says she is writing this to memorialize Dusty. She says it plainly. But the jail cell is unexplained. Why is she locked up? What did she do? The reader files these questions and moves on because Hen's voice is so commanding, so funny, so apparently forthcoming that it feels rude to press. This is the foundational misdirection: Hen's enormous personality — her digressions, her profanity, her whiskey-rotted charm — is not ornamentation. It is *load-bearing evasion*. She is performing candor with such energy that the reader does not notice she has skipped the single most important piece of information in the frame. Every entertaining aside from this point forward is a wall she is building between the reader and the answer to the question: *why are you the one in the cell and not in the ground?*

---

## Beat 2: The Meeting — "She Looked Like Trouble That Had Already Happened to Someone Else"

**Concrete Action:** Hen tells the story of meeting Dusty. The year is approximately 1873 (Hen is vague about dates, possibly deliberately). The setting is a failing settlement or trading post in New Mexico Territory. Hen is young, already practicing midwifery, already half-feral. Dusty arrives under circumstances Hen tells at least two different ways — first as a near-dead drifter Hen nursed back to health, then, crossed out and restarted, as a woman who walked into Hen's tent and stole her only good knife and Hen followed her to get it back and simply never stopped following. Hen cannot or will not settle on a single origin story. What is consistent in every version: Dusty was half-Apache, broke, ferociously smart, and looked at Hen like Hen was the answer to a question Dusty hadn't finished asking.

**Narrative Technique — The Competing Origin Myths as Emotional Seismograph:** The crossed-out, rewritten versions of the meeting are not gimmickry. They are the first place where the reader can begin to calibrate what Hen's revisions *mean*. Every rewrite shifts the power dynamic. In version one, Hen saved Dusty — she was the strong one, the caretaker. In version two, Dusty was the agent, the thief, the one who moved first. Hen can't decide which version to commit to because each version assigns a different *debt* — and the question of who owed whom is, we will eventually understand, the fault line that cracked their entire partnership. The reader should be taught here to read the *direction* of each revision. When Hen crosses something out, the deleted version is almost always closer to the truth. The replacement is almost always more flattering to Hen or more forgiving of what came later.

**What Makes It Memorable — The Knife Detail:** Regardless of which version, the knife recurs. It is the first concrete object in the friendship, and it should carry the same talismanic weight as Jackson's black box — shabby, functional, unremarkable at first glance, but eventually revealed as the object that contains the whole relationship's symbolic architecture. If the knife appears at the end (and it should), this moment retroactively becomes the most important scene in the story. Plant it like Jackson planted the stones: a detail that looks like texture and turns out to be the entire point.

---

## Beat 3: The First Con — "We Discovered We Were Both Liars and Neither of Us Had the Decency to Be Ashamed"

**Concrete Action:** Hen and Dusty execute their first scheme together. The specific con should be small-scale, almost comic — perhaps selling fraudulent land claims, or Dusty impersonating a Mexican nobleman's widow while Hen plays the grieving servant, or a rigged card game where they fleece a group of men too drunk or too proud to admit they were beaten by women. The important structural elements: (a) it works, (b) they are good at it, (c) they discover a shared fluency in deception that feels, paradoxically, like intimacy, and (d) Hen narrates this section with the most joy anywhere in the manuscript. She is *happy* here. The prose should feel different — looser, faster, funnier, more generous.

**Narrative Technique — The Private Language as Love Story:** This beat establishes the central relationship's grammar. Hen describes learning to read Dusty's signals across a room — a tilt of the chin, a specific cough, the way she'd tuck hair behind her left ear when the mark was ready to be closed. Hen narrates this with the same breathless precision that romance narratives use for the cataloguing of a beloved's body, but the lexicon is entirely criminal. The reader should feel the seduction, should understand that for two women in 1873 with no legal power, no wealth, and no social standing, the ability to deceive the world *together* was the most intimate act available. The cons are not just how they survived. The cons are how they *spoke*. Deception was their mother tongue, and the only honest conversation they ever had was conducted in it.

**What Makes It Memorable — The First Crossed-Out Confession:** Somewhere in this section, mid-celebration, Hen should start to write something and then cross it out. Something that begins to approach the real nature of her feeling for Dusty — not just friendship, not just partnership, but something she doesn't have nineteenth-century frontier language for, something the journal can't hold. The crossed-out sentence should be *almost* legible. The reader should be able to half-reconstruct it. This is the first time the journal's materiality becomes a narrative device: the physical act of deletion is itself a confession. What Hen can't say is louder than what she can.

---

## Beat 4: The Rise — "She Built an Empire Out of Absolutely Nothing True"

**Concrete Action:** A compressed, propulsive sequence — possibly structured as a list, a montage, or a series of vignettes Hen rattles off with the cadence of someone counting coup. Over a period of years (mid-to-late 1870s into the 1880s), Dusty accumulates cattle, land, influence. She forges documents. She impersonates officials. She bribes territorial bureaucrats. She exploits the chaos of post-Civil War land grabs and the Anglo legal system's contempt for Indigenous and Mexican land rights — and she does it as a half-Apache woman, which means she's playing a game that was designed to destroy her and she's winning it with the house's own loaded dice. Hen assists, enables, midwifes the entire operation. Hen also delivers actual babies throughout this period — she never stops being a midwife — and this double role should be woven in, not as comic relief but as structural counterweight.

**Narrative Technique — The Montage as Moral Anesthesia:** The compression here serves the same function as Jackson's procedural beats: it normalizes escalation. Each con is slightly larger, slightly more dangerous, slightly more morally ambiguous than the last, but because Hen delivers them with the same wry amusement and at the same narrative velocity, the reader absorbs them the same way. A forged deed and a stolen herd and a bribed judge all feel equivalent. The reader is being acclimated to lawlessness through *pacing*. Hen is doing to the reader exactly what she and Dusty did to the Territory: making the fraudulent feel routine. This is also where Hen's midwifery becomes thematically essential. She brings life into the world with her own hands, honestly, painfully, at genuine physical risk — and she does so *in between* acts of theft and fraud. The juxtaposition should never be commented on. Hen does not see a contradiction. The reader should be increasingly unsure whether there is one.

**What Makes It Memorable — The Moment Hen Stops Being Credited:** Buried in the montage, a shift occurs. Early cons are "we" — Hen and Dusty together. Gradually, the pronoun changes. Dusty begins to be the one who decides. Dusty's name is in the land records (false names, but hers). Dusty acquires a reputation. Hen becomes support staff. The shift should be narrated without bitterness — Hen presents it as natural, even jokes about it — but the reader should feel the asymmetry growing. The montage should end with a single sentence, almost a throwaway, in which Hen describes something Dusty did without consulting her. It should be small. It should feel like nothing. It is the first crack.

---

## Beat 5: The Rattlesnake in the Room — "I Should Have Said Something and I Did Not"

**Concrete Action:** A specific scene in which someone — an outsider, an enemy, a visitor, perhaps a lawman or a rival rancher or an old associate from the early con days — arrives and delivers a warning or a threat. Not vague menace: a concrete, legible signal that Dusty's empire is attracting the kind of attention that ends in violence. Dusty dismisses it. The critical structural requirement: *Hen sees the danger clearly*. Hen understands what Dusty does not — or what Dusty refuses to understand. And Hen says nothing. Or Hen says something small, something hedged, something that lets Dusty wave it away. This silence — this failure — should be the scene Hen has the most trouble narrating. The revisions here should be visible, frantic. Multiple starts. Multiple cross-outs. Sentences that begin "I told her—" and stop dead.

**Narrative Technique — Old Man Warner in Reverse:** Where Jackson gave us a character defending the ritual from the inside (Warner's "pack of crazy fools"), this story needs a character *breaking* the internal logic from the outside — someone who names plainly what Hen and Dusty have been refusing to see. But the structural trick is that this character should be *at least partly wrong* in their reasoning, or offensive in their manner, or compromised in their authority, so that Dusty's dismissal feels emotionally justified in the moment even though it's strategically suicidal. The reader should understand why Dusty doesn't listen. They should also understand that Hen *could have* made her listen and chose not to. This is the beat where the reader begins to suspect what Hen has been hiding: her complicity is not in the cons. Her complicity is in the *silence*.

**What Makes It Memorable — What Hen Crosses Out Here:** The most important deletion in the manuscript should occur in this section. Hen should begin to write the real reason she didn't push harder — the thing she was afraid of losing, the thing more important to her than Dusty's safety. It might be the partnership itself. It might be that speaking up would have required admitting she was not Dusty's equal but her dependent. It might be that the only way to warn Dusty was to break the private language they'd built, to speak plainly for the first time in twenty years, and Hen could not bear to do that because plain speech was what the rest of the world used. Whatever it is, Hen crosses it out. She replaces it with a joke. The joke should be very, very funny. And the reader should feel sick laughing at it.

---

## Beat 6: The Betrayal Hen Can't Stop Circling — "Here Is the Part I Have Written Four Times and Burned Three"

**Concrete Action:** Something Hen did, or failed to do, that directly contributed to Dusty's destruction. The specific action is the story's deepest secret and should be withheld until this beat. Possibilities: Hen gave information to someone — a lawman, a rival, an enemy — whether intentionally or through negligence. Hen was offered a way out and took it for herself but not for Dusty. Hen, in a moment of jealousy or resentment over the growing asymmetry of their partnership, allowed a threat to reach Dusty unimpeded. Whatever the action, it must be precisely the kind of thing Hen has been building the entire narrative to avoid stating. Everything before this — the funny stories, the argued-with reader, the whiskey-soaked charm, the aggressive unreliability — has been a fortification against *this paragraph*.

**Narrative Technique — The Structural Trap Snaps Shut:** This beat must pay off the specific contract you've built with the reader about the journal's material form. If Hen has been crossing things out, this is where the reader encounters a passage where critical words are *not crossed out but missing* — torn from the page, blotted beyond reading, deliberately destroyed. The narrative should break down formally. Hen's voice should fracture. Sentences should stop finishing. The reader has been trained to read Hen's evasions as charming; now the evasion is desperate, ugly
narrative_story:
# The Ballad of Dusty Marvell, As Best I Can Remember It

---

## I.

Whoever the hell finds this journal, I need you to understand three things before we go any further.

First: my name is Hen Pool and I am a midwife, which is to say I have pulled more screaming life into this world than anyone in Doña Ana County and been paid for approximately a third of it. I have delivered breech babies by candlelight. I have delivered twins in a rainstorm in a sodhouse where the roof was coming down in clumps and the mother was fourteen and the father was nowhere because fathers are almost always nowhere, which is the first thing you learn in my trade and the last thing you forget.

Second: I am a liar. I am a liar the way some women are left-handed — it is simply the orientation of my nature, and I came by it young enough that I cannot tell you where honest leaves off and the rest begins. I have lied to priests. I have lied to lawmen. I have lied in three languages, one of which I do not actually speak, which I suppose is a fourth lie stacked on whatever I was lying about in the first place. I tell you this not as a boast but as a courtesy. You should know what you are holding.

Third: Dusty Marvell is dead.

She has been dead for seven months. She died on the ninth of March, 1893, which was a Thursday, which was a cold day for the territory, and she died — 

She died and I am in this cell and the trial is in six days and this journal is the only paper they will give me because the lawyer, that wretched gap-toothed boy with the new collar, thought it would be *therapeutic* for me to write down my *feelings*. He actually said the word feelings. He said it the way you'd say *carbuncle* or *diphtheria* — like it was a medical condition he'd read about in a book and was now diagnosing from a safe and Christian distance.

So here are my feelings: I want whiskey, which they will not give me. I want a cigarette, which they will not give me. I want to stop dreaming about Dusty's hands, which were the most capable hands I have ever seen on a human body, man or woman, and which I will never see again because she is dead, which I have mentioned, which I will not stop mentioning, because if I say it enough times in enough ways perhaps it will finally lose its teeth and become just another fact I can set down and walk past.

It has not lost its teeth yet.

I do not expect you — whoever you are, wherever you are, whenever you find this moldering little book in whatever corner of whatever ruin — to believe what follows. I do not expect you to like me. I don't even expect you to read to the end. But I am going to tell it anyway, because there is nothing else to do in here but count the cracks in the adobe and listen to Deputy Boggs pick his teeth, and because Dusty Marvell lived, she *lived*, and the world should have at least one record of that fact even if the record is composed by a liar in a jail cell who can't be trusted to get the weather right.

Don't get comfortable.

This is not that kind of story.

---

## II.

I met Dusty Marvell in — 

The year was 1873. Probably. It may have been 1874 because I remember the Garza store had burned already and some people say the Garza store burned in January of '74, but other people say late '73, and I was not in the habit of writing down dates at that age because I did not yet own a calendar or a reason to care what day it was. Days were just weather then. You got up and the weather was a thing that happened to you and then it was dark and you went to sleep and the next weather started.

I was living outside the settlement of Los Huesos, which was not a town so much as a rumor that had accumulated some buildings. There was the Garza store before it burned. There was a cantina that served mescal that tasted like it had been strained through a saddle blanket. There was a post office that was really just a crate inside the cantina. There were perhaps forty people, depending on the season, roughly half of whom owed me money for delivering their children and roughly a quarter of whom were those children. I lived in a canvas-and-timber structure I will generously call a tent, and I owned: one mule, one set of midwifery tools wrapped in oilcloth, one copy of a anatomy text I had stolen from a dead surgeon's field kit during the war — not the fighting part of the war, the messy afterward part — a wool blanket, a coffeepot, and one good knife.

I need you to understand about the knife. It was not fancy. It was a skinning knife with a walnut handle that had cracked once and been bound back together with copper wire. My mother had used it and her mother had used it and I could not tell you the providence before that. It was not, by any empirical assessment, a valuable knife. It was not sharp enough. The balance was wrong. But it was mine, mine in the way that a thing can be yours when you have almost nothing — not a possession but an organ. An external heart. I would sooner have surrendered a finger.

This is how I met Dusty:

I was asleep and then I was awake and there was a shape in my tent and the shape had my knife. I could see it — the copper wire on the handle catching what little moonlight came through the canvas. The shape was moving toward the flap. I said, or rather screamed, something that was probably not a word, and I launched myself at the shape and we went down together in a tangle of limbs and blanket and the tent half-collapsed on us so that we were thrashing there in the dirt like two cats in a sack. I got a fistful of hair. The shape got an elbow into my stomach. I bit something — an arm, I think — and the shape said, very clearly, very calmly, in a voice like smoke over gravel: "You bite hard for someone so skinny."

I said — and this I remember exactly, because it was the first honest thing I said to her — "Give me back my knife, you [piece of shit], or I will bite a lot harder."

She laughed. She was lying under me in a collapsed tent with my teeth marks on her forearm and she *laughed*. And then she said: "I'll trade you. The knife for a meal. I haven't eaten in two days."

So I fed her.

~~That is not exactly how it happened.~~

~~What happened was I found her. She was half a mile south of Los Huesos in a wash, face down, not moving. I thought she was dead. She was not dead. She was sun-sick and starved and her lips were cracked to bleeding and she had a gash on her left calf that was going the color of a bruise that means the blood underneath has started to give up. I brought her water. I cleaned the wound. I fed her broth for two days from a jackrabbit I'd snared, spooning it into her like she was one of the babies, and on the third day her eyes opened all the way and focused on me and she said~~

No.

That is not right either. Or it is right but it is not *true*, which is a different thing, a thing I have never been able to explain to anyone who has not lived it. You can get every fact correct and still lie with the shape of them, the order, the weight you give each one. A midwife knows this. A birth told as *the baby came and the mother wept with joy* is a different creature than the same birth told as *there was a lot of blood and the cord was wrapped and I thought for a full minute we were going to lose them both and then we didn't*, even though both versions happened, both are true, both are the same twelve hours in the same room.

What is true, in every version, in every way I have tried to tell this to myself in the years since:

She was half-Apache on her mother's side and something else on her father's — Mexican, maybe, or some mix she never pinned down and did not care to investigate because her father was a gap in her history she kept sealed shut, the way you'd board up a well that had gone poisonous.

She was broke the way only people who understand money can be broke — not ignorant of it but emptied of it, scraped out, the way a mine is broke after you have taken everything that glitters and left nothing but the shaft.

She was smart the way a river is fast. You did not experience her intelligence as a quality she possessed. You experienced it as a current, and you were either swimming with it or you were drowning.

She took my knife. That part is true in every version. She took it and I followed her and I have spent twenty years trying to decide if I ever got it back or if I just stopped noticing it was gone because the hand that held it had become more interesting than the knife itself.

She looked at me — this is the last thing I will say about the meeting because I am aware I am stalling — she looked at me the way I have seen certain women look at a locked door. Like I was the answer to a question she hadn't finished asking. Like she was still constructing the question. Like the answer had shown up early and she was annoyed and curious in equal measure.

I did not know what to do with that look.

I should tell you: I still don't.

---

## III.

The first job we ever did together was the Peralta claim, and it was so stupid it should not have worked, and it worked beautifully, and I have never been happier in my life before or since, and if that is a pathetic thing to say about a land fraud I committed at the age of — at whatever age I was — then I invite you to go to hell because you did not feel what I felt and you do not get to judge the venue where I felt it.

Here is how it went.

There was a man named Horace Blunt. There is always a man named something like Horace Blunt. He had come out from St. Louis with capital and very clean boots and a conviction that the New Mexico Territory existed specifically for the purpose of making him rich. He wanted land. He wanted a great deal of it. He particularly wanted a parcel along the river south of Los Huesos that was, at the time, being used by a handful of families — Mexican families who had been there long enough that the dirt knew their names — but Horace Blunt did not recognize the claims of people who could not produce the right papers in the right language in the right office, which is to say Horace Blunt did not recognize the claims of people who were not Horace Blunt.

Dusty heard about this in the cantina. I don't know who told her. People told Dusty things. She had that quality — you wanted to offer her information the way you'd offer a pretty woman a drink, just to see if she'd take it, just to be part of whatever she was going to do next.

She came to me with the bones of it and I fleshed it out. That was how we worked, from the very beginning. She was the architect. I was the — what is the word — the contractor. The one who knew where the nails went.

The plan: we would sell Horace Blunt a land grant. Not the actual land grant, which did not exist in any form he could use. A *better* land grant. One we would make ourselves. Dusty had a hand like a printer's — she could reproduce any signature, any seal, any official flourish, after seeing it once. I was the one who knew what the documents should *say*, because I could read English, Spanish, and enough legal Latin to fake the rest, and because I understood — here is where the midwifery comes in, oddly — I understood what people needed to see in order to believe something was alive. A birth certificate and a land grant are not so different. Both are pieces of paper that insist a thing is real. The baby does not need the paper. The land does not need the paper. But the world will not acknowledge either without it.

We forged a grant. We aged it with coffee and careful tearing. We invented a genealogy for the grant — a chain of title going back to the Spanish crown, complete with a family named de Peralta that had never existed outside of Dusty's handwriting and my imagination. We decided I would present it because I was white and plain-faced and had the kind of trustworthy forgettable look that authority relies on, and because Dusty — Dusty *could not* present it, for reasons that had nothing to do with ability and everything to do with the particular ugliness of who is believed and who is not in a Territory that was three different countries' stolen property depending on which century you held up to the light.

This is something I need you to understand. I need you to understand it now because it will matter later and I will not be in the mood to explain it later: Dusty was better than me at everything. *Everything*. The forgery, the reading of men, the strategy, the nerve. She was better and she could not walk into Horace Blunt's office and be believed because she was a brown woman with cheekbones that told the truth her mouth never would about where she came from. So I walked in instead. I was the face. She was the mind. And this arrangement — which we never discussed, which we did not need to discuss, which was as obvious and as rotten as the weather — this arrangement was the first brick in a road I am still walking and it led here, to this cell, to this page, to the fact that she is dead and I am the one with a pencil.

But I was telling you about being happy.

Horace Blunt bought the grant. He paid in cash and land scrip and the deed to a small warehouse near the river, which Dusty later sold to a man from Tucson for twice what it was worth. The families along the river kept their homes — we made sure, or Dusty made sure, which I suppose is the same thing except it isn't, except it should be. Horace Blunt did not discover the fraud until months later in a territorial office in Santa Fe, at which point he was too embarrassed to pursue it, because admitting you were swindled by two women in Los Huesos was a social death no amount of St. Louis capital could resurrect you from.

We celebrated. Dusty bought mescal — the good kind, from below the border, not the saddle-blanket variety — and we sat outside my tent and drank it and the stars were obscene, as they always are in that part of the country, and she told me about a con she'd seen as a child, a man in Tucson who had sold the same horse to three different buyers in the same afternoon by simply never letting any two of them see the same side of the animal. She told it with her hands, acting out the parts, and the firelight was on her face and her mouth was loose from the mescal and I thought— 

~~I thought, this is the only person who has ever~~ 

~~I wanted to tell her that she was the~~

She told the story and I laughed and we drank more and I remember the specific quality of the happiness. It was not soft. It was not warm. It was *bright*, it was the happiness of having found the one other person in the world who spoke your language, the language under language, the one that is not taught but *recognized*, and I had spent my whole life up to that point certain that I was the only native speaker and here she was, fluent, and what I felt was not — it was not what you might think, it was not that simple, and even if it was I do not have the vocabulary for it, this language was not built to hold what I — 

It doesn't matter what I thought.

We were partners. That is the word I will use. We were partners and we were brilliant at it and the world was going to regret letting us find each other.

---

## IV.

I do not have the patience or the paper to tell you everything we did in the years that followed, so here is the brief accounting, the way you'd read a ledger if the ledger was written by a woman who was there for all of it and is now trying to fit a decade into a few pages because the alternative is remembering each moment individually and that is a thing I cannot do from this cell without losing what is left of my composure.

*1875, spring:* Dusty acquires forty head of cattle through means I choose not to detail except to say that the previous owner was a man who had himself acquired them through means I choose not to detail, and so on, back through a chain of theft so long that the cows themselves probably could not have identified their original provenance. We drive them south and sell them to a broker who does not ask questions because he has arranged his life specifically around the not-asking of questions.

*1875, fall:* I deliver the Sandoval twins.

Write a chapter following a young diplomatic envoy sent to address tensions on a distant human colony where humanity has diverged into distinct subspecies through both natural adaptation and separation of lineages. Against protocol, the envoy slips away from official functions to walk the streets alone, encountering markets, ordinary citizens, and social structures that contradict the official briefings. A challenging conversation ensues, in which the envoy's wits and will are tested, by a seasoned political operator looking to test the mettle of the offworlder.

The envoy’s cloak draws curious stares from locals who dress more minimally. Length: 1000 words.
